grammar.explanation: This pattern introduces the name of a person, place, or thing: a noun called or named something.

grammar.key: grammar:い形容詞の語幹+くなる
grammar.pattern: い形容詞の語幹＋くなる
grammar.explanation: This pattern changes an adjective into a description of becoming that way. It expresses a change in strength, frequency, or another quality.
This pattern presents an action as completed, often with regret or an unfortunate result. Here it emphasizes the tragedy of the deaths.
This pattern describes a change in what happens or what someone can do. Here it means that the ghosts began appearing.
This pattern lists representative actions without implying that they are the only actions performed.
This pattern expresses the aim of preventing something from happening. The following quotation marker conveys the intention behind building the temple.
This pattern makes the affected person or thing the focus: something is called, built, written, guided, or cut by someone, often without naming the agent.
This pattern connects two actions performed by the same person at the same time, meaning while doing something.
This pattern means to make, let, or have someone do an action. Here it describes singing for people to hear and having Hoichi play.
This pattern presents an arrangement or outcome that comes about through circumstances. Here Hoichi comes to live at the temple.
This pattern means even if or even though, indicating that the following situation holds despite the preceding condition.
This pattern expresses an impression or inference, meaning seems to be. Hoichi judges what is around him from what he hears.
This pattern is a direct, familiar request or command asking someone to do something for the speaker.
This pattern means in accordance with or exactly as described. Here it means doing as the warrior says.
This pattern expresses obligation, meaning must or have to. Its past form describes an obligation that applied in those days.
This pattern gives a blunt command. It is used to order the gate opened and to relay the master's order to perform.
This pattern attaches a verb meaning begin to another verb's stem, expressing the start of that action.
This pattern means increasingly or even more, showing that a quality becomes stronger.
This pattern describes a gradual change over time.
Attached to a verb's negative stem, this pattern expresses necessity or obligation: must do something.
This pattern introduces a result that contradicts what the preceding situation would lead one to expect.
Following a verb's negative stem, this pattern politely asks someone not to do something.
This pattern introduces a term as the topic of a definition or explanation.
This pattern lists representative actions. Here the listed actions are followed by a conditional ending, warning against either action.
This pattern means at least this much, presenting a limited amount as the minimum acceptable option.
Attached to a verb stem, this pattern shows that the same person performs two actions at the same time.
Used with a negative predicate, this pattern means never again.
This pattern expresses a change into a new state or customary situation. Here it describes coming to be known by a new name.

patternSegments.text: 〜なくてはならない／〜なければならない

grammar.explanation: This pattern expresses obligation: someone must do something. It combines a negative condition with a statement that the alternative is unacceptable.
This pattern means doing one action while doing another. Both actions have the same subject.
This pattern expresses an uncertain possibility, meaning might or may.
This pattern makes a courteous request, meaning would you please do something for me.
This pattern describes trying to do something or being about to do it.
This pattern presents an action as something done for another person's benefit. It can imply that the recipient has lower status.
This pattern means characteristic of or befitting the person or role named by the noun. Its negative form means unbecoming of that role.
This pattern connects an action to something left undone, meaning without doing that other action.
This pattern respectfully describes another person doing something for the speaker's benefit. Here the woman confirms that Umetsu will hold the child for her.
This pattern says that an action has only just happened. Here it describes a newborn baby.
This pattern describes a subjective impression, meaning to feel as though something is the case.
This pattern means to try an action to see what happens or what can be discovered.
This pattern describes a state continuing unchanged. Here the baby remains small.
This pattern expresses completion, often with regret or an unintended result. Here it also appears in an intentional thought about dropping the baby.
This pattern expresses a strong conclusion meaning that something must be the case.
This pattern expresses obligation: someone must do something.
This pattern expresses a change continuing into the future or movement progressing away or onward. Here the baby continues growing heavier.
This pattern means however much or no matter how, indicating that the result remains the same despite the degree of a condition.
This pattern presents an appearance or comparison meaning as though or just like.
This pattern combines a verb's volitional form with an attempt or imminent action, meaning to try to do or be about to do something.
This pattern credits someone or something for a favorable result, meaning thanks to.
This pattern adds another person or thing to the first, meaning not only one but also another.
This pattern expresses strong wonder or admiration in an exclamation about how remarkable something is.
This pattern means just as or in accordance with. It follows a past-tense verb directly or a noun linked by a possessive particle.
This pattern embeds a yes-or-no question inside a larger sentence, meaning whether or not.
This pattern means to try doing something to see what happens or find something out.
